9ded31d2996bd774: MUMBAI, Oct 21 — Billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Jio Platforms attracted enough investor bids to fully subscribe its initial public offering within two hours of opening today, putting India’s likely biggest-ever listing on track.

Jio Platforms, which houses the country’s biggest wireless operator and is the digital services arm of Ambani’s Reliance Industries, is looking to raise up to US$3.2 billion (RM13 billion) in India’s most anticipated IPO this year.

Bids placed by investors exceeded the 197.5 million shares on offer within 100 minutes of opening, according to BSE stock exchange data, with local media calling it the “fastest-ever subscribed IPO” in India.
Most analysts expect gains when the stock debuts in Mumbai next week — likely October 28 — despite the weak performance of Indian equities this year.
Launched a decade ago, Jio’s wireless service disrupted the market with steep discounts that helped it rapidly win customers from rival telecom firms Bharti Airtel and Vodafone.
The company’s 533 million subscribers provide a “strong foundation for future growth”, analysts at financial services firm Motilal Oswal said in a note.
But they also cautioned that “monetisation of newer digital services” still needs to be “demonstrated at scale”.

While the massive IPO is seven years in the making, it comes at a challenging time for Reliance — India’s most valuable listed company, which still depends heavily on its traditional oil business to make money.

Reliance’s refining empire drew the anger of the United States last year after White House adviser Peter Navarro accused Indian tycoons of profiting off the Ukraine war by buying discounted Russian crude.

While Navarro did not identify specific businessmen, it was widely seen as a swipe at Ambani, who appeared this year to offer an olive branch by supporting the construction of America’s first major new oil refinery in half a century.

Ambani is set to meet US Secretary of State Marco Rubio today in the western city of Jamnagar — where Reliance’s massive refinery complex is located — as Washington seeks to boost energy cooperation with India.
Experts say Jio is key to Reliance’s strategy to evolve beyond its oil business and the touchstone of its future tech ambitions.
While Jio makes most of its money from telecoms, it has expanded into areas including artificial intelligence.

Reports also said it was also considering a low-orbit satellite constellation to provide internet services from space — a venture that would see it compete with Musk’s Starlink, which has been trying for years to launch in India.
Musk accused unnamed Indian “oligarchs” this month of preventing Starlink’s rollout in the country, and referred to the Reliance boss as “Prime Minister Ambani” and the “real boss of India”.
Reliance responded by noting that it had never “feared competition” and welcomed offerings from rivals in satellite communications, including Starlink. — AFP
62b8596ce978c7e0: GEORGE TOWN: All educational institutions in the state will operate as usual tomorrow despite the haze affecting the country.
The Penang Education Department said it would continue monitoring air quality and prioritise the safety, health and well-being of students and education personnel.
"We remain concerned about the safety and health of students amid the deteriorating air quality," it said in a statement.
The department said students attending school are encouraged to wear face masks as a precaution and drink sufficient water to stay hydrated.
It said schools must also ensure an adequate supply of drinking water is available for students and staff.
Parents or guardians concerned about their children's health due to the haze may consider keeping them at home, provided they inform the school administration, it added.
b26097a61323ee58: SEPANG: The usually quiet courts complex was abuzz as Malaysia Border Control and Protection Agency (MCBA) director-general Datuk Seri Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain arrived to face charges of voluntarily causing hurt to two Special Branch policemen.

At the entrance, Rela personnel manning the gate held up signs informing the media and the public that parking within the court complex was prohibited, directing them to park along the roadside instead.
Shuhaily, 54, arrived at 7.30am in a dark suit, accompanied by a convoy of several cars and outriders.
Among those present in a show of solidarity was Port Klang MCBA commander Datuk Nik Ezanee Mohd Faisal.
The entourage headed straight to the canteen, where they occupied several tables for breakfast.
When photographers gathered outside the canteen to photograph Shuhaily through the windows, he invited them to join him for breakfast, joking that he "would not have a salary after this".
Given the anticipated crowd, the proceedings, initially scheduled to be heard at the magistrate's court, were moved to a larger Sessions Court on the upper floor of the complex.
More than 10 journalists were allowed into the public gallery, while the remaining benches were occupied by Shuhaily's supporters.
A nine-member legal team, led by Datuk Rosal Azimin Ahmad, appeared for Shuhaily.
Magistrate Khairatul Animah Jelani presided over the case, which began shortly after 9am.
As Shuhaily was charged as a summoned person, he stood near the dock as the court interpreter read out the two charges against him.
Listening attentively, with his hands clasped behind his back, he told the court that he understood the charges and claimed trial.

The two charges alleged that he had voluntarily caused hurt to Lance Corporals Muhammad Ekmal Sofwan Driman, 25, and Mohamad Faiz Saman, 40, at Counter J on the fifth floor of KLIA Terminal 1 between 1.27pm and 1.35pm on Sept 28.
The charges were framed under Section 323 of the Penal Code, which provides for a maximum jail term of one year, a fine of up to RM2,000, or both, upon conviction.
During submissions on bail, Shuhaily's legal team described the case as an unusual one involving a police commissioner.
The prosecution countered that it was not unprecedented, citing the case involving former Inspector-General of Police Tan Sri Abdul Rahim Mohd Noor.

The tense atmosphere in the courtroom briefly eased when defence co-lawyer Kitson Foong argued that Shuhaily was not a flight risk, quipping that he was the man tasked with guarding the country's borders.
The remark drew laughter from the public gallery.

Shuhaily was also represented by lawyers Datuk Yaacob Md Sam, Datuk Ahmad Zaidi Zainal, Muhammad Rafique Rashid, Md Yunos Shariff, Datuk Akberdin Abdul Kader, Datuk Baljit Singh Sidhu and Dr Badruzzaman Ishak.
The proceedings lasted close to an hour, with the defence and prosecution making submissions on bail.

The prosecution sought bail of RM5,000 with one surety for each charge, arguing that the amount was reasonable and not excessive, while the defence sought Shuhaily's release on a personal bond without bail.
The court set bail at RM1,500 with one surety for each charge and ordered Shuhaily to attend future proceedings, without imposing any additional conditions.
Following the proceedings, Shuhaily was seen entering a holding room adjacent to the courtroom.
He emerged about 40 minutes later after a family friend posted bail, accompanied by his lawyers, who then held a press conference.
Earlier, before being charged, Shuhaily had told the media that he would refrain from making further comments on the case after the proceedings.
He is scheduled to return to court on Nov 25 for mention.

06d966964ba49556: SEOUL, Oct 21 — North Korea has moved new units into “firing positions”, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un said today, days after Pyongyang warned it was considering deploying additional strike means to its border with South Korea.

Tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang have soared since the South last month blamed an explosion inside the heavily fortified Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) separating the two countries on landmines laid by North Korea, an accusation it has rejected.
“Our military leadership underlined the need to make those rogues aware that our new firepower units have taken their firing positions,” Kim Yo Jong said, according to state media.
Her statement came a day after Seoul warned of a “firm” response to further North Korean provocations.
She added that Kim Jong Un had “issued an order to fortify the border with an enemy state to be eternally impregnable”.

The statement came as the Korea Central News Agency said the armed forces’ Marshal Pak Jong Chon had inspected “pivotal positions” on the border, stressing to troops it was “time to organise the firepower strong enough to strike terror into the enemy’s heart”.

“If the enemy troops make a provocation actually threatening the safety of our service personnel... The border forces of the DPRK must take very proficient, specialised and overwhelming military action,” he said, using the acronym for the North’s official name.

Seoul’s military accused Pyongyang yesterday of attempting to shift the blame for escalating military tensions, while confiming it had used both loudspeakers and warning shots as “legitimate defensive measures to prevent North Korean troops from crossing the MDL (Military Demarcation Line) and to drive back troops that have crossed it”.

Jin Yong-sung, chairman of South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, ordered the military to “respond with firm resolve” should North Korea use Seoul’s actions as a pretext for aggressive action, while the defence ministry warned they would be met with “resolute” punishment.

North Korea has separately tested a slew of weapons recently, including a “new-type” precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to employ AI technology. — AFP
b335f615f867a96d: KUALA LUMPUR: Westports Holdings Bhd's net profit rose 26.4 per cent to RM342.56 million in the third quarter ended Sep 30, 2026 from RM271.11 million in the same quarter last year backed by higher revenue.
Its revenue rose 42.1 per cent to a record RM1.07 billion in the quarter under review from RM751.99 million previously due to a tariff increase and stronger value-added services revenue.
For the nine-month period, Westports' net profit rose to RM1.03 billion from RM725.2 million last year while revenue rose to RM2.83 billion from RM2.06 billion.

In a filing with Bursa Malaysia, the port operator said the global interest rate environment has pivoted upward since last quarter as cumulative inflationary pressures have reached financial markets after energy prices spiked again.
"Nevertheless, consumption propensity has remained resilient despite such headwinds, as technology-related investments have supported economic development and growth optimism," it said.

It added that the group's transhipment volume reflects how liners navigate and capitalise on the evolving regional supply chains and growing economic requirements, whereas gateway reflects domestic containerised requirements.
"The group now expects overall container throughput to be at least the same as the previous year, but fast-evolving conditions could still materially affect the volume outlook," Westports said.
87f65209a4bc235c: JELI: A security guard was killed when a tree fell on him while he was riding his motorcycle in Kampung Ayer Lanas.
Mohd Alia Sabri Mat Repin, 40, suffered severe head injuries and died at the scene.
Jeli Fire and Rescue Station chief Mohd Adni Ibrahim said 10 firefighters were dispatched to the scene, where they found the victim trapped beneath the fallen tree.
"The victim worked at Jeli Polytechnic and was riding a Honda EX5 motorcycle from his home in Bukit Bunga to his workplace when the incident occurred.
"Dashcam footage from a road user showed the tree falling and striking the victim," he said.
Mohd Adni said firefighters, assisted by Civil Defence Force personnel, used a chainsaw to cut the fallen tree and remove the victim.
9ed2eb32a6a2e958: KUALA LUMPUR: The Registration of Criminals and Undesirable Persons (Amendment) Bill 2026 was tabled for its first reading in the Dewan Rakyat today.
Deputy Home Minister Datuk Seri Dr Shamsul Anuar Nasarah, while tabling the bill, said it would be presented for its second reading during the current sitting.
The bill seeks to provide for the particulars of a person convicted of a registrable offence to become spent.
Clause 2 seeks to amend Section 2 of the Act to introduce the definition of "crime-free period" for the purposes of the new provisions relating to registrable particulars becoming spent.
Clause 3 seeks to introduce new sections 13a, 13b and 13c into the Act.

The proposed new section 13a seeks to provide for registrable particulars becoming spent, including the eligibility requirement, applicable crime-free period and circumstances under which the registrable particulars cease to be eligible to become spent.
The proposed new section 13b seeks to provide for the effect of registrable particulars of a person convicted of a registrable offence becoming spent.

Upon the registrable particulars becoming spent, the registrable particulars shall be treated as no longer registered in the register and as if the person has not been convicted of the registrable offence to which the spent registrable particulars relate.

The new section 13b further provides that even though the registrable particulars have become spent, the registrable particulars shall remain recorded in the register for the purposes of record by the registrar.

The proposed new section 13c seeks to provide that the registrable particulars of a person which has become spent shall be revived if during or after the expiry of a crime-free period, the person is convicted of any registrable offence specified in the First Schedule.

The proposed new section also seeks to provide that if the registrable particulars of the person is revived, the registrable particulars of the person shall be treated as if they have never become spent under the Act.

Clause 4 seeks to amend subsection 15(1) of the Act to empower the minister to amend the proposed new Fourth Schedule, while Clause 5 seeks to introduce a new Fourth Schedule to provide the list of registrable offences for which registrable particulars are not eligible to become spent.
The bill will not involve the government in any extra financial expenditure.
d1cbbf878953af4b: HONG KONG, Oct 21 — The former father-in-law of murdered Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi bought a meat mincer just 13 days before her death — and even enquired about a bone-crushing machine before deciding its HK$35,000 (RM18,200) price tag was too steep, a court has heard.

In chilling testimony at the Hong Kong High Court yesterday, a kitchenware shop assistant described how Kwong Kau, 68, selected a more expensive meat mincer capable of grinding meat more finely, along with an assortment of oversized cooking equipment.
The purchases were made on February 8, 2023, less than two weeks before Choi, a 28-year-old model and influencer, was allegedly murdered and dismembered in a case that horrified Hong Kong.
Kwong is standing trial alongside his sons, Choi’s former husband Alex Kwong, 31, and former brother-in-law Anthony Kwong, 35, over her killing.
According to The Straits Times, the shop assistant, who testified anonymously, told the court that a white-haired man entered the shop at around noon on February 8.
CCTV footage confirmed the customer was Kwong Kau.
After examining several meat mincers, he chose a pricier model that could supposedly produce a finer mince.
He also bought a large soup pot measuring 14 inches by 14 inches, a 15-inch chopping board and an 11-inch ladle.
The bill came to HK$9,153, reduced to HK$8,700 after a discount.
The assistant explained that the shop primarily supplied restaurants and catering businesses, accounting for the unusually large equipment.
Then came an even more unsettling enquiry.
After a younger man arrived, Kwong asked whether the shop sold a machine capable of crushing bones.
But when told it cost approximately HK$35,000, the two men decided it was too expensive and left without buying one.
The testimony came on the 19th day of the trial into Choi’s death.
Her dismembered remains were discovered at a Hong Kong village house on February 24, 2023, three days after prosecutors allege she was murdered.
The three defendants are charged with murder and preventing the lawful burial of her body. All three deny murder, while Alex and Anthony have pleaded guilty to preventing lawful burial.
The court also heard claims about Choi’s apparent financial difficulties from her former chauffeur, Chin Kei Shun, who said the socialite’s spending habits had changed in the months before her death.
Chin, hired in May 2021 on a monthly salary of HK$20,000, said Choi previously carried large amounts of cash but later occasionally asked him to pay for shopping purchases before reimbursing him.
He also recalled an incident in February 2022 when two or three men were seen lingering outside Choi’s home, prompting her to hide inside his vehicle as he drove into the compound.
Chin linked the incident to gambling debts allegedly incurred by Choi and her partner, Chris Tam, in Macau.
He also claimed to have overheard Choi asking Anthony Kwong for HK$600,000 during a telephone conversation.
Days later, Chin drove Anthony to a shopping mall to collect an envelope allegedly containing that amount.
The following day, he drove Choi to another mall, where she was carrying what he described as the same envelope.
Choi went to meet Kwong Kau but returned to the vehicle without it, he testified.
Chin also told the court that he resigned in November 2022 after Anthony asked him to take two months of unpaid leave while the family travelled.
Questioned about his conduct, Chin denied allegations of theft and abusive language, and said he had never discussed gambling with the Kwong family.
He acknowledged previous drug possession convictions in 1998 and 2024, saying he had completed a one-year probation order for the latter offence.
The trial continues.
d0c050d850877c27: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 21 — The capital’s public housing schemes are receiving a major aesthetic and safety facelift, with City Hall (DBKL) foregoing garish paint schemes for neutral tones while overhauling critical electrical infrastructure across dozens of ageing buildings.

Speaking during a working visit to People’s Housing Programme (PPR) Taman Mulia in Bandar Tun Razak today, Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Federal Territories) Hannah Yeoh said that DBKL made a deliberate shift away from the bright, multi-coloured exteriors long associated with government flats.
Accompanying her on the site inspection were Kuala Lumpur Mayor Datuk Seri Fadlun Mak Ujud and Bandar Tun Razak MP Datuk Seri Dr Wan Azizah Wan Ismail.
“I would like to add that the colours chosen by DBKL are neutral colours, for the residents to know that this is a residential area and not a kindergarten.
“Many PPRs have been colourful, so we have chosen neutral colours,” she said.
Aside from the cosmetic exterior refresh, Yeoh said that the priority remains addressing life-threatening structural risks.

DBKL partnered with the Institution of Engineers Malaysia to conduct comprehensive technical audits across public housing schemes and municipal flats citywide, targeting deteriorating electrical risers and wiring to avert catastrophic fire hazards.

At PPR Taman Mulia, DBKL committed RM6.67 million in restorative works for roughly 2,128 residents. The project includes RM3.48 million towards repainting the towers, RM2.55 million to replace sub-main cabling and main switchboards, RM370,000 for internal road resurfacing, and RM272,000 to modernize fire prevention systems.

Mayor Fadlun said the citywide rehabilitation drive is moving steadily, with around 70 per cent of targeted projects completed. DBKL set 64 public housing sites for refurbishment in 2026, aiming to cross the 80 per cent completion line before year-end.
“The rest has been allocated for the 2027 budget, which we will continue for the PPRs and PAs that are not ready,” he said.

Fadlun further noted that Putrajaya has earmarked RM446 million in total for upgrading works across public housing estates and municipal flats, tailoring allocations to the specific infrastructural deficits of each scheme.

To ensure financial governance, DBKL plans to erect transparency signboards at individual housing estates displaying line-item expenditure, giving residents a clear accounting of public funds spent on their blocks.
Dr Wan Azizah reminded the community that structural improvements require civic responsibility, urging residents to safeguard shared amenities and combat vandalism.

“I see improvements, mainly in the PPRs area. However, what I would like to suggest is to take care of the infrastructure,” she said, noting that upkeep is indispensable if families are to enjoy secure and dignified living quarters.

Built in 2002, PPR Taman Mulia houses 912 residential units across two 21-storey towers. Having clocked more than two decades of heavy wear and tear, key mechanical and electrical fixtures required substantial rehabilitation to maintain habitability standards.
The estate was handed over to its Joint Management Body (JMB) on Dec 1, 2025, alongside a professional management agent to handle day-to-day estate administration.
DBKL reiterated that preserving public housing standards depends on continuous cooperation between the municipality, building managers, and resident committees.
ca46debd179caa5f: KUALA LUMPUR: CIMB Group Holdings Bhd is weighing a privatisation of its Indonesian arm, CIMB Niaga, as market volatility dims prospects for a secondary share offering.
The second-largest Malaysian bank by assets is also considering a placement of CIMB Niaga shares to strategic investors, analysts said.

The options follow revised minimum free float rules requiring the group to reduce its 91.4 per cent stake in CIMB Niaga to no more than 87.5 per cent by March 2027 and 85 per cent by March 2028, as Indonesia seeks to improve the investability of its stock market.

However, the prospect of MSCI downgrading Indonesia from emerging market to standalone market status has triggered a broad sell-off in Indonesian equities, weakening the appeal of new share offerings.
Public Investment Bank Bhd analyst Wong Ling Ling said the privatisation proposal remained at a "preliminary stage with regulatory hurdles to overcome".
"The group remains optimistic on CIMB Niaga's operations, with growth predominantly driven by wealth management, selected SMEs as well as Shariah banking," Wong noted.
PublicInvest estimated that buying out CIMB Niaga's minority shareholders could cost about RM800 million.
Hong Leong Investment Bank said a privatisation could simplify CIMB Niaga's ownership structure and give CIMB greater flexibility to execute its longer-term strategy in Indonesia.

"While the eventual structure remains unclear, we believe a Niaga privatisation could still require some deployment of group capital, particularly if the chosen structure involves buying out part of the remaining minority interests," it added.
0a37374aa675cb40: JOHOR BARU: A 20-year-old man was found still using his MyKid as an identification document, claiming repeated attempts to obtain a MyKad failed due to documentation issues.
The man was found during the National Registration Department's (NRD) Op Jejak 1.0 at a printing factory in Pasir Gudang yesterday.
The man, who lives with his aunt in Pasir Gudang, said his first MyKad application at the age of 12 was unsuccessful due to documentation issues involving his biological father's details.
He said another application submitted several years later was rejected over problems with his adoption documents.
"This is the only identification document I have. My employer said I could use it, so I thought there would be no problem.

"I only studied until Year Five, so I never encountered any problems without a MyKad. When I applied for this job four months ago, my employer said I could use my MyKid. I did not realise it was an offence," he said.
The man was among 234 individuals inspected during the operation, including 137 Malaysians.
Officers are conducting investigations after he failed to produce documents proving he previously applied for a MyKad.
NRD deputy director-general (operations) Sarinah Apisah said such cases were suspicious and could involve issues in birth registration records.

"When a case reaches this stage, resolving it becomes complicated and time-consuming. We will explore various avenues, including tracing siblings to conduct DNA testing if necessary," she said when met during the operation.
Sarinah said the department would expedite the man's MyKad application if the information he provided was verified.
Meanwhile, 36 foreigners were detained during the same operation on suspicion of using forged identity cards or those belonging to other individuals to secure employment in Malaysia.
Sarinah said the detainees comprised 28 women and eight men, aged between 16 and 48, believed to be from the Philippines and Indonesia.
439f0036d01df497: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 21 — Taobao Malaysia has launched its 11.11 Global Shopping Festival, offering free shipping on 400 million products and introducing new artificial intelligence (AI) tools to improve the cross-border shopping experience.

The campaign runs from October 20 to November 13, 2026, and provides Malaysian consumers with access to over three billion products across various categories, including fashion, home living and furniture.
Taobao Malaysia Country Head Jess Lew said the platform aims to offer high-quality products at greater value while simplifying the shopping journey.
“Today’s consumers are looking beyond basic necessities. They are seeking quality products that reflect their interests and lifestyles,” she said in a statement.

She added that the platform has continuously invested in localising the experience, which includes introducing Bahasa Malaysia and English interfaces, partnering with local payment providers, and strengthening customer service.
“The expansion of our local return network is another important step towards giving consumers greater confidence and convenience when shopping across borders,” Lew said.
To assist shoppers, the platform is rolling out four AI-powered features.

These include an AI Try-On feature for visualising clothing, an AI Shopping Assistant for personalised recommendations and price comparisons, AI Product Insights for summarising reviews and specifications, and a Voice-Search-by-Hold tool for users who cannot find the right keywords.
In addition to the digital enhancements, Taobao is expanding its local logistics network.
Starting in November, the platform will introduce more than 1,400 local return drop-off points across Malaysia in collaboration with J&T Express.
This service aims to allow shoppers to return eligible purchases domestically without needing international shipping.
The campaign also features several promotions and savings for consumers:
Up to 15 per cent off sitewide through official platform discounts
Daily air shipping discount vouchers at 12pm and 8pm
Exclusive up to RM50 RHB Bank instant rebates for eligible cardholders
Up to RM8 waiver in payment processing fees
Up to RM40 in new users’ perks
Platform vouchers offering up to 50 per cent off for English app users

As home improvement gains traction among Malaysian consumers, Taobao has made more than 1 million furniture items, including sofas, dining tables and height-adjustable desks, eligible for direct shipping to Malaysia.

During the festival, shoppers can also grab up to RM30 in furniture shipping vouchers on eligible purchases, which is complemented by compensation protection for damaged items via Taobao Official Logistics.

To build excitement beyond the digital space, Taobao is bringing the campaign offline through activations at Lalaport Kuala Lumpur on October 24 and 25, and at Xiamen University Malaysia on October 27 and 28.

These events build on the platform’s recent partnership with popular actor Zhang Linghe, including the newly launched Zhang Linghe-themed app interface and daily treasure hunt campaign, giving visitors the chance to engage with interactive experiences and redeem exclusive themed merchandise.
For more information on the Taobao 11.11 Global Shopping Festival, consumers can follow Taobao Malaysia on Facebook, Instagram and TikTok, or visit the app.
c643b74d3397f564: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 21 — Individuals who misuse their identity cards (MyKad) by ‘renting out’ or handing them over to foreign nationals could face up to three years in prison, a fine of up to RM20,000, or both, Deputy Home Minister Datuk Seri Dr Shamsul Anuar Nasarah said.
He said the National Registration Regulations 1990 provide strict legal measures to curb foreign nationals’ misuse of national identity.

“The government takes this matter seriously, with enforcement aimed not only at penalising offenders but also at preventing identity misuse and identifying such cases at an early stage,” he said during a question-and-answer session in the Dewan Rakyat today.

He was replying to a supplementary question from Mohamad Shafizan Kepli (GPS-Batang Lupar) about reports of some Malaysians renting out their MyKad to foreign nationals for only RM100 to work in factories.

Mohamad Shafizan had earlier highlighted the detention of 36 foreign factory workers in Pasir Gudang during Ops Jejak 1.0 yesterday for allegedly using fake MyKad or those belonging to other people to gain employment.
Shamsul Anuar said the operation underscored the importance of joint enforcement efforts by the National Registration Department (NRD), the Immigration Department and Labour Department.

“The operation also focused on the possible involvement of original identity card holders suspected of renting out or handing over their documents to foreign nationals for employment purposes,” he said.
On enforcement efforts, he said the NRD had carried out 4,174 operations nationwide from 2022 to September this year, resulting in 1,868 arrests.

He said 577 cases were prosecuted under Regulation 25(1)(e) of the National Registration Regulations 1990 during the same period, comprising 449 cases involving the use of fake MyKad and 128 involving the use of others’ identity cards. — Bernama
b11b76b269db429d: SINGAPORE, Oct 21 — Little Trevor Neo was a cheerful baby who rarely cried, loved being carried and always wanted someone to hug him.
But behind closed doors, the eight-month-old was being shaken, smothered and beaten by the very parents he depended on for love and protection.

Now, as his parents face lengthy jail terms over his death, Trevor’s grandmother and aunt have recalled the smiling little boy they adored — and their disbelief that his father could have subjected him to such cruelty.
“He always wanted people to hug him,” his aunt told The Straits Times after the couple were sentenced at Singapore’s High Court today.
Trevor’s father, Neo Jia Ming, 27, was jailed for 16 years, while his mother, Chloe Gan Ci Xuan, 23, received 15 years and three months over the abuse and death of their son in September 2024.
The couple had pleaded guilty on October 12 to charges arising from the abuse. Neo also admitted to repeatedly assaulting his wife.
For his family, the revelations have shattered their image of a hardworking young father who juggled jobs to support his wife and child.
“It doesn’t seem like what my brother would do. Till now, I’m still not able to accept it,” Neo’s 29-year-old sister said.
His 64-year-old mother, who gave her surname as Koh, said she had encouraged him to marry Gan after learning of her pregnancy because she believed he should take responsibility for the baby.
The young couple even researched parenting before Trevor’s arrival.
Neo worked as a food delivery rider and pet groomer, while Gan was also a pet groomer before leaving her job after giving birth.
His elder sister occasionally helped with milk powder, diapers and money, but otherwise believed her brother was managing his responsibilities.
At family dinners, neither parent gave any indication that anything was seriously wrong.
“They only said they were tired,” Koh recalled.
Koh, who works at a coffeeshop in Hougang, said she rarely saw her grandson because of conflicting work schedules.
But her memories of Trevor remain vivid.
“He was very obedient and always smiled. He never cried. He had a face like a ‘big biscuit’,” she said in Mandarin.
Koh said she had bathed Trevor a few weeks before his death and noticed neither bruises nor anything unusual about his condition.
The family also had no reason to suspect Gan was being abused.
The couple appeared inseparable, with Neo’s sister recalling that her brother doted on his wife and even saved money to leave Trevor with a nanny so they could take short holidays together.
But court documents revealed a very different relationship.
Between February and August 2024, Neo repeatedly assaulted Gan, including punching her at an arcade because she had played a game without him.
On another occasion, he punched her at a bus stop after she accidentally led them onto the wrong bus.
Trevor, meanwhile, endured repeated abuse, with his parents shaking him and covering his mouth and nose to stop him from crying.
Gan struck the baby on numerous occasions, while Neo slapped his son, dug his fingers into the child’s mouth and hit him.
He also repeatedly pinched Trevor’s fingers to provoke a reaction, which he found amusing.
The couple exchanged messages discussing the abuse and even joked about the possibility that shaking the baby could cause brain damage.
The violence culminated on September 1, 2024, when Gan smothered Trevor, struck him in the face and placed him face down on a mattress.
The infant was pronounced dead at KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital shortly after midnight on September 2. Both parents were arrested after hospital staff alerted police.
For Trevor’s grandmother, what remains is the memory of a smiling little boy who loved being carried.
“He was very obedient and always smiled. He never cried. He had a face like a ‘big biscuit’,” she recalled.
7954902f524d0017: KUALA LUMPUR: The FA of Malaysia (FAM) must repair its tarnished reputation before seeking recognition or expecting sponsors to place their confidence in the association, says football analyst Sadek Mustafa.

He said the fallout from the heritage player scandal continued to overshadow Malaysian football, with questions being raised over FAM's nomination for the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) Member Association of the Year (Gold) award.

French investigative journalist Romain Molina recently questioned the nomination, given FIFA's sanctions against FAM and seven players in 2025 over falsified documents used to establish the players' eligibility to represent Malaysia.
Sadek said FAM should have concentrated on putting its house in order and restoring public confidence before pursuing awards.

"The image of Malaysian football is still tarnished and FAM should not have applied for the AFC award as a sign of repentance. Only once everything is in order and results are being produced, should they seek recognition through awards," he said.
He said FAM still had considerable work to do to clear its name following the scandal, which triggered FIFA sanctions and the resignation of its executive committee.

The association is also trying to strengthen its commercial backing, with FAM media and marketing committee chairman Datuk Syed Mahadi Syed Hassan saying on Monday that it was close to securing partnerships with two major local companies.
Sadek welcomed the prospect of fresh sponsorship but said the details should be made public once the agreements were signed.
"It is positive, but we hope more details will be revealed after the signings are confirmed," he said.

FAM disclosed in August last year that it had raised between RM7 million and RM8 million against a sponsorship target of RM15 million, highlighting the financial challenge facing the association and its national teams.

Its commercial relationships also came under scrutiny after the FIFA sanctions, with long-time sponsor Bank Islam having sought an explanation from FAM. The association was fined 350,000 Swiss francs (about RM1.8 million) over the case.
Meanwhile, Sadek called on FAM to explain its staff retrenchment exercise, which has already attracted public criticism, including from former FAM marketing head Sayf Ismail.
He said the national body should clarify the reasons behind the cuts and ensure the process complied with Malaysian labour laws.

Sadek also questioned whether reducing the workforce would make FAM more efficient, warning that cost-cutting could prove counterproductive if it focused on lower-paid employees without addressing broader operational needs.
"It will be pointless to be penny-wise and pound-foolish if only the low-paid staff are removed," he said.
d84a96f0c07b5259: KUALA LUMPUR: Pas president Tan Sri Abdul Hadi Awang has accused an unnamed Perikatan Nasional (PN) component party of turning its back on the coalition, while insisting ties among the remaining parties remain strong.
He said PN's administration and management had been conducted in accordance with the coalition's constitution, despite the Registrar of Societies' (RoS) decision to cancel its registration.
"All aspects of PN's administration and management have been carried out properly and in accordance with the coalition's constitution.
"Harmony among the component parties remains very strong, except for one party that has distanced itself and turned its back on the coalition," he said in a statement.
Hadi did not identify the party he was referring to.
His remarks come amid strained relations between Pas and Bersatu, with both parties having contested against each other in previous state elections.
Earlier, Pas deputy president Datuk Seri Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man told the New Straits Times that the two parties had not cooperated since the Johor and Negri Sembilan elections.
He confirmed that Pas and Bersatu would again face each other in the Melaka state election, while Pas would maintain its electoral understanding with Umno.
Meanwhile, Hadi condemned the government's alleged role in PN's deregistration, describing the decision as an attempt to restrict democratic rights.
He expressed disappointment that the decision had been made before the court could rule on PN's legal challenge.

"Pas regrets this action, which appears to pre-empt the court's decision, restrict democratic rights guaranteed under the Constitution and reflect growing fear on the part of the government," he said.

Hadi said Pas would continue working with like-minded PN component parties to determine its next course of action, including preparations for the Melaka state election and legal proceedings to challenge the deregistration.
He also thanked party members, supporters and undecided voters who hoped for a change in the country's leadership, while urging all parties to respect the law and democratic principles.
PN, formed in 2020 following the Sheraton Move, had its registration cancelled under subparagraph 13(1)(c)(iv) of the Societies Act 1966.
RoS said the coalition's representations submitted on Oct 12 had failed to refute the grounds for cancellation outlined in its Sept 22 notice.
The Melaka state assembly was dissolved on Sept 23, with polling scheduled for Nov 14.
The Election Commission has fixed Oct 31 for nominations and Nov 10 for early voting.
ba3dafbb6fc721a6: KUALA LUMPUR: Perlis could be heading towards another change of menteri besar or even a snap state election, as the suspension of Abu Bakar Hamzah threatens to reignite the Pas-Bersatu power struggle.

Political analysts said the latest turmoil had exposed unresolved tensions dating back to last December's leadership crisis, with the future of the state government hinging on whether Abu Bakar retains majority support.

Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities director Associate Professor Dr Mazlan Ali said the latest developments could lead to another change of menteri besar or the dissolution of the state assembly.
He said the political crisis, which saw eight Perikatan Nasional (PN) assemblymen withdraw support for then-menteri besar Mohd Shukri Ramli, had left deep divisions between Pas and Bersatu.
"The three Pas assemblymen and five Bersatu assemblymen withdrew their support for the Pas menteri besar, and Abu Bakar was subsequently appointed to replace him.
"Pas viewed this as a betrayal because Bersatu was its political ally at the time, yet acted in a manner the party considered unacceptable," he told the New Straits Times.
Mazlan said Abu Bakar's suspension could stem from alleged breaches of Bersatu's internal regulations, although the precise reasons for the disciplinary action remained unclear.
He said the development should also be viewed against the wider breakdown in relations between Pas and Bersatu.
"The possibility of the menteri besar resigning or the state assembly being dissolved cannot be ruled out.
"I believe Pas has the political advantage because Abu Bakar's position has become uncertain following his suspension," he said.
He said Pas could potentially regain control of the state government if a fresh election were held.
He said that Pas currently held six seats in the state assembly, compared with Bersatu's five and Pakatan Harapan's one, with three seats vacant.
However, he said the party had so far refrained from challenging Abu Bakar's appointment, possibly out of respect for the Raja of Perlis, who had consented to his appointment.
Mazlan said the breakdown in Pas-Bersatu relations would be difficult to repair, particularly following PN's deregistration.
"The political compromise may no longer be sustainable following PN's deregistration.
"There is a possibility of the state assembly being dissolved or another change of menteri besar," he said.

Universiti Malaya sociopolitical analyst Professor Datuk Dr Awang Azman Awang Pawi said the latest dispute showed that last December's leadership change had failed to resolve underlying disagreements between Pas and Bersatu.
"The issue should have been resolved with the appointment of a new menteri besar, but disputes over power-sharing and trust between the parties have persisted.
"It may be a leadership issue, but I believe it is also linked to Pas-Bersatu relations and how these are managed in Perlis," he said.
Awang Azman, who is also a National Unity Advisory Council member, said Abu Bakar's political survival depended on his ability to retain majority support in the state assembly.
He said Pas had a numerical advantage over Bersatu but remained divided, making cooperation among its assemblymen crucial.
"Pas has a numerical advantage, but unfortunately, they are not united.
"If the Pas assemblymen can work together, they would have an advantage in choosing their own menteri besar.
"The question now is the relationship between the assemblymen, the Pas central leadership and the Raja of Perlis," he said.
He warned that a vote of no confidence could pose a greater threat to the state government's stability than Abu Bakar's suspension itself.
Meanwhile, International Islamic University Malaysia political scientist Associate Professor Dr Syaza Shukri said Abu Bakar's suspension should not be viewed solely as an internal
Bersatu disciplinary matter.
She said it also reflected the continuing struggle for political influence between Pas and Bersatu since the change of menteri besar in December 2025.
However, Syaza cautioned that the disciplinary action did not automatically remove Abu Bakar from office.
She said the crisis could result in a political compromise, a realignment of assembly support or another change of menteri besar.
She said the outcome would ultimately depend on political negotiations and the actual balance of support in the assembly.
The latest turmoil comes less than a year after Abu Bakar, the Kuala Perlis assemblyman, was sworn in as menteri besar on Dec 28, 2025, replacing Pas' Mohd Shukri.
The leadership change followed the reported withdrawal of support for Mohd Shukri by eight PN assemblymen, comprising five from Bersatu and three from Pas.
Pas subsequently terminated the membership of the three assemblymen, and their seats were declared vacant.
Bersatu suspended Abu Bakar's membership rights for two party election terms, effective Oct 13.
The action was reportedly taken after he breached Clause 9.1.4 of the party constitution and its Code of Ethics and Conduct.
The latest development also comes after the Registrar of Societies cancelled PN's registration on Oct 20.

65191396c3a83137: OCTOBER 21 — We spend millions educating young Malaysians to think critically, yet the moment one asks an uncomfortable question, we seem more interested in questioning the student than answering the question. What an extraordinary contradiction! Our universities proudly advertise critical thinking, intellectual freedom and independent judgment as essential graduate qualities. Yet when these qualities are demonstrated beyond the safety of classroom discussions, they suddenly become controversial. Have we been teaching our students to think, or merely training them to know when to keep their mouths shut?

The recent public reaction to a university student's question concerning fundraising to help former Prime Minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak pay a fine exposes something far more troubling than the question itself. It reveals how uncomfortable we have become with independent thinking, particularly when it challenges political loyalties, established beliefs or public sensitivities. Whether we agree with the student is beside the point. The real issue is whether Malaysia genuinely wants graduates who can think for themselves or simply individuals who have mastered the art of saying what others want to hear. If asking an uncomfortable question is enough to provoke public outrage, perhaps it is not the student's maturity that needs examining, but our own.
General view of Universiti Malaya in Kuala Lumpur, January 22, 2024. — Picture by Firdaus Latif

Walk into almost any Malaysian university and you will hear familiar promises. We want graduates who think critically, challenge assumptions, solve problems and demonstrate intellectual independence. These ambitions appear in university brochures, course outlines and national education policies. But how seriously do we practise what we preach? We praise students for asking questions in classrooms, yet become uncomfortable when those questions involve political figures, public institutions or sensitive decisions. Is critical thinking only acceptable when everyone agrees with the question? A university should not be a place where students learn which opinions are safe to express. It should be where they learn how to examine competing opinions intelligently.

One dangerous habit in public discussions is assuming that asking about an issue automatically means supporting or opposing it. A student questioning a fundraising initiative is not necessarily defending or condemning the person involved. The student may simply be seeking clarification, examining its implications or inviting discussion. Unfortunately, we are becoming increasingly quick to judge people's intentions rather than examine their arguments. Instead of asking whether a question is reasonable, we ask whose side the person is on. This habit discourages genuine discussion and encourages intellectual laziness. Of course, asking questions does not automatically make someone a critical thinker. Questions can be poorly framed, based on incorrect information or driven by personal bias. But that is precisely why education matters. Lecturers should help students examine evidence, question assumptions, recognise different perspectives and reconsider their conclusions. Silencing an imperfect question teaches very little. Examining it teaches considerably more.

The educational philosopher John Dewey argued that meaningful thinking requires examining beliefs through evidence and reflection. In simple terms, intelligent people do not merely defend what they believe. They are willing to ask themselves whether their beliefs could be wrong. Imagine if every university classroom encouraged students to ask three simple questions: What is the evidence? What am I assuming? Could there be another explanation? These questions would strengthen not only academic learning but also public discussions. Malaysia needs citizens who can question public spending, examine government policies, recognise misinformation and disagree without resorting to personal attacks. However, we cannot expect such citizens to emerge from an educational culture that rewards agreement more readily than independent judgment.

Perhaps we have been asking the wrong question. Instead of asking whether students are mature enough to raise controversial issues, perhaps we should ask whether our institutions and society are mature enough to respond to them. Disagreement is not automatically disrespect. Questioning authority is not necessarily rebellion. Defending someone's right to ask does not mean agreeing with their views. Responsible freedom requires accurate information, respectful discussion and a willingness to accept criticism. These standards should apply equally to students, academics, politicians and the public. Ultimately, the strength of a university should not be measured by how successfully it avoids controversy, but by how intelligently it handles disagreement.

Malaysia does not need graduates who merely know the correct answers to examination questions. It needs citizens who know which questions must be asked, even when those questions make others uncomfortable. If our universities produce graduates who are afraid to question, have we educated them to think, or merely trained them to obey?
* This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
02500ad999e8e657: MUMBAI, Oct 21 — India’s film industry, where scenes featuring nudity or sex often rely on improvisation and mutual trust, is gradually welcoming professionals tasked with choreographing intimacy to protect actors and ensure consent.

Once unheard-of in Bollywood, intimacy coordinators are becoming an increasingly familiar presence on sets as filmmakers embrace stricter standards after the #MeToo movement put a spotlight on sexual exploitation in entertainment industries around the world.
The shift comes as streaming platforms have pushed storytelling into a more nuanced territory, creating greater demand for realistic portrayals of sexuality.

“Just like a stunt director handles a fight scene... for scenes of intimacy, we map out exactly where the hand goes and where the hair goes so nothing is left to awkward improvisation,” said Aastha Khanna, one of a small but growing group of intimacy coordinators in Bollywood.
Most arrive on set armed with “modesty tools” that allow performers to simulate intimacy while minimising unnecessary physical contact.
A typical kit includes crotch guards, nipple pasties and doughnut cushions, which ensure a safe distance between performers during sex scenes.
The emergence of such coordinators reflects a broader transformation in an industry where intimate scenes traditionally relied on trust between actors and directors, often with few formal safeguards.
Khanna said coordinators are usually hired before casting begins.
“The idea is that actors know there are intimate scenes in the script and can decide whether they are comfortable with them before signing on,” she told AFP.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This photograph taken on September 16, 2026 shows intimacy director and BraveSpaces Creative India founder Neha Vyaso (right) demonstrating a protective silicone modesty pouch used by male artists to actor Dev Surana during a mock intimacy workshop for an upcoming project in Mumbai. Once unheard in Bollywood, such coordinators are becoming an increasingly familiar presence as filmmakers embrace stricter standards after the 2017 #MeToo movement put a spotlight on sexual exploitation in entertainment industries around the world. — AFP pic
No longer ‘taboo’
Bollywood, one of the most prolific movie-making machines in the world, largely sidestepped physical intimacy on screen for decades because of strict government guidelines and powerful censors.
Kissing and sex were implied symbolically, with flowers brushing against each other, crashing waves or a crackling fire standing in for overt desire and consummation.
Even when filmmakers pushed the boundaries, the mechanics of filming intimate scenes remained largely unstructured.
Among the first mainstream Hindi productions to formalise the practice of intimacy direction was Gehraiyaan, backed by filmmaker Karan Johar and released on Amazon Prime Video in 2022.
Intimacy coordinator Khanna worked to establish personal boundaries and choreograph scenes, while intimacy coach Neha Vyaso conducted workshops focused on physical dynamics and consent.
This model has gradually spread across productions meant for streaming services, which industry experts say have been the primary drivers of change.
“There’s much less censorship and more openness to stories that explore taboo subjects,” Vyaso said.
Crime drama franchise Mirzapur, known for its graphic content, started off without intimacy coordinators in its early seasons.
But lead actor Rasika Dugal said such specialists fill a critical gap.
“In the initial seasons, we had to navigate boundaries individually based on personal comfort,” she said.
“It is very important to have intimacy coordinators so nobody is violated in any way and everyone’s concerns are properly taken care of.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This photograph taken on September 16, 2026 shows intimacy director and BraveSpaces Creative India founder Neha Vyaso (right) conducting a mock intimacy workshop with actors Priti M (centre) and Dev Surana for an upcoming project in Mumbai. — AFP pic
Emotional scars
Bollywood’s glamorous exterior long concealed a chaotic backstage culture where personal boundaries were routinely crossed.
“There have been instances where the actor ended up kissing his co-star without her consent. We ensure that none of this happens in the flow,” Khanna said.
But professionals like her remain far from universal, numbering just over a dozen across India’s film and television industries.
In many commercial blockbusters, there is not much scope for their expertise because major actors often avoid explicit physical intimacy or even kissing on screen.
Certain films feature intimate scenes without a dedicated coordinator, while some experienced directors continue to manage scenes themselves.
With no formal guidelines or any requirement to hire an intimacy coordinator, some in the industry hope film associations will eventually introduce industry-wide standards.
To Khanna, the role of a coordinator extends well beyond simulated sex.
“A scene of intimacy is not necessarily just a spicy or a romance scene, it is a much larger umbrella” that can encompass violence, dominance, harassment and nudity, she said.
“The work that I do mitigates a situation where a person may go through several years of therapy and the scar may not heal.” — AFP
d55de8e145206e3b: MELBOURNE, Oct 21 — Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs removed, her husband told journalists today, after what police called a “targeted” attack.

Haines is in a stable condition at a Melbourne hospital after being struck by a car on Monday near her office in the town of Wangaratta, more than 200 kilometres (120 miles) northeast of the Victoria state capital.
Speaking at the hospital today, her husband Phil said that surgeons had been forced to remove both her legs.
“But the good news in all this is Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family,” he said.
“The two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind,” he said.
“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person.”
The man alleged to have wounded Haines, in what police have called a “targeted” attack, faced court earlier today.

Police have charged 43-year-old Brendan Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury, as well as the federal crime of harming a public official, which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.
He has also been charged with cultivating a cannabis plant and possession of the drug, according to court documents shared with AFP.
Nugent appeared at a courthouse in Wangaratta, an AFP journalist at the scene said.
He did not apply for bail and his next hearing is scheduled for February 4.
‘Extremist views’

The alleged attack has sparked soul-searching in a country where political violence is rare, but where police have documented a steady rise in threats and abuse towards elected officials in recent years.
Governor-General Sam Mostyn — King Charles III’s official representative in Australia — said the nation was crying out for “decency” following the attack.
“Australians are yearning for kindness and care, and they’re asking us why we’ve lost the great skill of disagreeing well,” Mostyn said alongside Helen’s husband Phil.
The motive remains unknown and authorities have refused to speculate while the investigation takes place.
But police said today they were examining all possible leads, including that Nugent may have held radical anti-government views.
“Like everyone, we’re examining social media associations, talking to witnesses, friends and colleagues,” Victoria police commissioner Mike Bush told journalists.
Bush said authorities held no intelligence on the suspect and had seen nothing to suggest he posed an immediate threat before the attack.
Australian Federal Police (AFP) Commissioner Krissy Barrett said there was a growing level of “extremist views” online.

“The current criminal threat environment is febrile and when it comes to federal parliamentarians, the AFP continues to record the growing volume of online abuse, threatening rhetoric and intimidation,” she said.
World ‘more dangerous’
The independent lawmaker, 65, was standing near the trunk of her car when she was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser on Monday afternoon.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has led an outpouring of support for Haines, who was widely praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.
He bemoaned the fact that political debate in Australia had grown too heated and personal over the past few years.
“It’s a reminder that the world is a more dangerous and divided place than it was a generation ago,” Albanese told ABC Melbourne radio today.
“I think that Australians do want to see their politicians be able to go about their business, to be able to get something from the back of their car, for goodness sake.”
Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action. — AFP

3a7b0650e95ace77: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia must establish a clear roadmap for the 2030 World Cup-2032 Asian Cup qualifying campaign, with the ageing national squad making it urgent to plan for the next generation, says analyst Datuk Richard Scully.

With the national team's average age at 32.5 years, Scully said the FA of Malaysia (FAM) and Malaysian Football League (MFL) need to work together to build a stronger player pool instead of relying on short-term fixes.
The challenge, he noted, is creating a clear pathway from youth football to the senior squad, ensuring promising players gain enough competitive exposure to handle international football.

"The M-League's heavy reliance on foreign imports has limited opportunities for young Malaysians. The league needs to be restructured to ensure clubs give emerging players meaningful playing time," Scully said.
"We can argue that younger players can play in the lower leagues, but it is not the right platform for them to improve due to the lower intensity and wider gap compared to the international level.
"We need to make an Under-23 slot compulsory in the M-League. A team should field at least one Under-23 player on the pitch so they can gain valuable top-flight experience."
Scully said MFL should collaborate with FAM's technical director on a comprehensive development plan that identifies potential long-term prospects and outlines their preparation programme.

Malaysia's Under-20 squad, who qualified for the 2027 Under-20 Asian Cup in China, could form part of that project, with Scully stressing the need to nurture young talent and provide a direct pipeline into senior international football.
The squad, guided by Shukor Adan, emerged as one of the seven best runners-up after collecting two points from draws against Indonesia and Australia in the qualifying round in Laos last month.

However, developing the next generation must go hand in hand with resolving the senior team's head coaching situation, appointing a full technical team, and giving the coach sufficient time to execute the plan, Scully added.
Malaysia, currently led by interim head coach Tan Cheng Hoe, finished third in the recent FIFA-Asean Cup after defeating Vietnam 1-0 in the third-place playoff at the Gelora Bung Karno on Oct 5.
With the head coach position still unconfirmed by the national body, Scully stressed that whoever takes the helm must be given ample support and patience.

"We tend to sack coaches after just a few matches. We have to understand that friendly matches are part of the broader preparation process," said the former Football Coaches Association of Malaysia (FCAM) vice-president.

b5e1dff0c005e0fa: TAIPEI, Oct 21 — Taiwan’s intelligence agency said China has cranked up cyberattacks and the distribution of misleading information against the island democracy ahead of local elections next month.
China claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has long threatened to use force to bring it under its control.
Taipei, which rejects that claim, accuses China of using cyberattacks, disinformation and espionage to erode people’s confidence in the Taiwanese government.

Taiwan was hit with an average of 2.6 million cyberattacks a day in the first nine months of 2026, and that has intensified since June, the National Security Bureau said in a report submitted to parliament yesterday.

China’s “cyber army” hit Taiwan’s academic and research sectors, telecommunications, and defence supply chains to interfere “with the Taiwanese government’s defence operations, undermine international cooperation, and steal sensitive technologies”, the report said.
Chinese cyberattackers are making use of artificial intelligence, including “AI agents to scan for vulnerabilities on our government websites”, it said.

Intelligence officials collected more than 2.5 million pieces of disinformation disseminated by China’s ruling Communist Party over the nine months, compared with around 1.7 million in the same period last year, mainly on Facebook and Threads.
Analysis indicates that the party has “utilised diverse channels”, including technological and human, “to influence the support preferences of our voters and the election results”, the report said.
Taiwanese voters go to the polls on November 28 to elect city and county government officials. — AFP
8c9dc395e791460b: THE tractors rolling into the town of Gela on the southern tip of Europe are flying the Sicilian flag, emblazoned with Medusa, three bent legs and ears of wheat, a reminder of the island's role as a breadbasket since Roman times.
But the farmers are not bringing in a harvest. They are protesting.

As soaring fuel prices squeeze household budgets and businesses across Europe, cost-of-living pressures are driving unrest and giving fresh momentum to far-right parties ahead of elections next year in countries including France, Italy and Poland.
Parties once considered fringe had already been gaining ground, with voters from motorists in rural France to young men in Germany's former Communist east looking for alternatives.

The US-Iran war, which erupted in February and sent energy prices sharply higher, has compounded the challenge for governments already struggling to contain inflation, support growth and rein in spending.
The discontent has spilled onto the streets.

In France, demonstrations that began over deteriorating school facilities in Paris' northern suburbs have morphed into some of the country's worst unrest in decades, with shops looted, buildings torched and a 19th-century town hall in Limoges set on fire.
"Why am I here? Well, quite simply, I find the current cost of living truly terrifying," said Quentin Leviloux, a 21-year-old protester in Nantes.
"Just think of people who earn barely the minimum wage, when you look at the cost of food, fuel, and everything else. It's terrifying how incredibly expensive things have become."

The European Commission estimates the Iran conflict has cost Europe roughly €100 billion (US$112 billion) through disrupted trade and energy markets. Gas prices have jumped about 140 per cent and diesel prices have doubled.

In a weekend address, French President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the "legitimate demands" of protesters angered by rising living and fuel costs, while condemning those responsible for violence and looting.
"We must never confuse them with those who destroyed, vandalised and looted," he said.

Violence has also erupted elsewhere. In the wealthy northern Italian city of Milan, police clashed on Sunday with protesters hurling stones and looting stores during demonstrations over poor public services and rising living costs.
In Gela, on Sicily's southern coast, farmers say fuel costs have made operating machinery prohibitively expensive. "We cultivate the land, we harvest debts," said one banner.
"We are completely at a standstill," said Arcangelo Gambino, a farmers' representative in Caltanissetta province. "The (fuel) cost has more than doubled."
Roadblocks by truckers, farmers and steelworkers have disrupted transport across parts of southern Italy, contributing to local fuel shortages and concerns over supermarket supplies.
Tens of thousands marched through Lisbon on Saturday over low wages, housing costs and the rising cost of living, increasing pressure on Portugal's centre-right government.
In Spain, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home sparked nationwide demonstrations over housing shortages and soaring rents, helping trigger a snap election next month.
Belgium has also seen demonstrations, while large rallies in Albania have been driven by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
The protests reflect broader economic anxieties that are increasingly shaping politics across the continent.
Concerns about purchasing power have become "a major driver of populist politics" across Europe, said Gilles Ivaldi, a political scientist at Sciences Po.

Politicians on both the hard right and hard left have increasingly argued that restoring energy ties with Russia would help lower costs, challenging Europe's mainstream consensus on support for Ukraine.
The latest energy shock comes after years of economic strain following the pandemic and the fallout from Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

In France, rising energy costs have provided an explosive backdrop to next April's presidential election. Macron's government is struggling with a ballooning budget deficit and pressure from bond markets.
Frontrunner Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally and hard-left veteran Jean-Luc Melenchon have both made fuel prices central planks in their campaigns.
"Rising fuel prices are clearly an issue that boosts Marine Le Pen," said Ivaldi. "I think this is an issue she has owned for quite some time."
Since the Iran war began, Le Pen's ratings have improved while Macron's have slipped, according to polling by Elabe.

Le Pen's proposal to sharply cut value-added tax on fuel has attracted broad public support. Analysts say the issue resonates strongly with her core voters in rural and semi-rural areas where car travel is often essential.
In neighbouring Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading national opinion polls after strong gains in local elections.
The cost of living topped Germans' concerns for a fifth straight year in a survey published this month.
German inflation spiked to nearly a three-year high in September, with energy price inflation rising to 14.9 per cent, handing ammunition to the AfD to attack Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The AfD is pushing to restore energy ties with Russia, arguing that Berlin's support for Ukraine is needlessly self-sabotaging at a time when Europe's largest economy and many of its energy-hungry companies are struggling.

Past experience indicates a link between high energy prices and voter turnout for the AfD, said Jan Steckel, professor for the political economy of climate change at the Technical University of Munich.
"Populist parties often frame energy costs as avoidable and attribute them to government policy choices ... rather than to the underlying geopolitical shocks that drive them," he said.
"These geopolitical shocks are ... much more difficult to explain. And I think this is why incumbent parties often struggle."
The argument is gaining traction elsewhere.

2d01364fd2510c7c: NEW YORK, Oct 21 — US photography company Getty Images said today it has commenced legal proceedings at a US bankruptcy court, as part of a previously announced plan to restructure its debt and take the firm private.

“The company has launched a solicitation process for formal approval of the prepackaged plan of reorganisation and, to implement the plan in the most efficient manner, has commenced voluntary Chapter 11 proceedings in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware... for certain of its US entities,” Getty Images said in a press release.
Getty, which partners with AFP among numerous other media companies, said this month that it had reached an agreement with major lenders and would undertake a “pre-packaged” bankruptcy.
The deal will see members of the Getty Family and affiliates of Koch Equity Development invest up to US$533 million (RM2.2 billion) to pay down debt, the company said.

Today, the company said it “has moved forward to implement its previously disclosed financial restructuring,” adding that it expects to complete the process “by year end after customary regulatory approvals are obtained.”
Getty will continue to operate normally throughout the process, citing up to US$143 million in financing from Koch, as well as cash from ongoing business.
Once the restructuring is complete, Getty will be a privately held company owned by the equity investors, it said.
Getty disclosed in a securities filing this month that it had been notified of plans to delist its shares from the New York Stock Exchange because they had fallen below US$1.
Getty reported a loss of US$206.1 million in 2025. — AFP

Pada 2023, Zahid diberikan DNAA bagi 47 pertuduhan rasuah dalam kes Yayasan Akalbudi selepas pihak pendakwaan memaklumkan keputusan itu dibuat bagi membolehkan Suruhanjaya Pencegahan Rasuah Malaysia menjalankan siasatan lanjut.

6393797ad96af2ab: KYIV, Oct 21 — When the air raid alert sounded over the Kyiv region, children knew exactly what to do: they grabbed their tiny backpacks and ran towards the shelter, abandoning bikes, toys and even a doll on the school playground.
Teachers scooped up the stragglers and ushered them into the shelter’s entrance, while the cleaner scanned the playground, muttering as she checked that no one had been left behind.
“Everyone to the shelter, quickly, quickly, quickly!” said Valentyna Kurinna, director of the UMKA primary school in Kyiv’s suburbs.
The risks weighed heavily on everyone’s minds.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photograph shows a school damaged following a Russian ballistic missile attack in Kyiv on October 19, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. — AFP pic
Just a few days earlier, a drone slammed into the same playground, narrowly missing a grandfather who stayed outside while the children had taken cover underground.
Security camera footage obtained by AFP showed him looking at the sky and running away just a few seconds before the explosion unleashed a huge ball of fire that burned the multicoloured playground.
Other videos from an empty classroom showed the blast blowing out windows, knocking out chairs and sending shards of glass across the room.
Four and a half years into Russia’s invasion, many people in the Ukrainian capital choose to ignore the air raid sirens — but at schools, they seek shelter every time.
Moscow used to hit the city mainly at night but now also attacks throughout the day, making the exhausting routine of repeatedly shepherding children in and out of shelters part of daily life.
On the day AFP visited the school, air raid alerts rang out five times between 7:30 am and 5:00 pm.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Schoolchildren attend a class in a shelter in the basement of UMKA Primary School during an air raid alert in the suburbs of Kyiv on October 20, 2026, amid Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. — AFP pic
‘When things are scary’
Within minutes, all the school’s 130 children were carrying on with their classes underground.
Yasya, Varvara and two girls both named Anya — 11-year-old friends since kindergarten — huddled around a table.
Practically jumping off the bench to speak to journalists, they suddenly became more shy when the camera turned to them.
“We can hug each other when things are scary. We can comfort each other with words too,” Varvara said.
It also helped to reminisce, including about an episode they called “The Flood”, when they accidentally flooded the bathroom during a sleepover, the memory of which left them in stitches.
Explaining the rules in case of air raid alert, they become serious.
“We all go to the shelter together and stay with each other,” Anya said.
“I don’t understand why we stay so close together,” she said. “At the same time, we’re supposed to run to the shelter as quickly as possible.”
Kurinna, the school director, worked hard to keep panic from setting in.
“We have no right to show that we’re scared. We have to smile, hug the children and reassure them,” she said.
Teachers also had to manage the fears from parents. They sent updates on group chats, posting emoji-filled messages saying “we are safe!” and photos of their children doing schoolwork underground.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Schoolchildren eat lunch in the canteen of a shelter located in the basement of UMKA Primary School during an air raid alert in the suburbs of Kyiv on October 20, 2026, amid Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. — AFP pic
‘Freedom!’
The UMKA Grand School, a high-level private school, is an exception in Ukraine.
In the capital, only 40 per cent of schools have shelters with sufficient capacity for all pupils, city hall told AFP.
Even those are often ill-equipped.

Parents have increasingly appealed to the education watchdog since air raids have become longer and more frequent, complaining of poor conditions including a lack of drinking water or access to toilets.
With private funding and an underground space, UKMA was lucky.
After the start of the war, staff quickly transformed the underground space — initially meant to welcome a music school.
The shelter has four different entrances to allow all the children downstairs smoothly, and spans several rooms and corridors with desks for everyone.
In a separate room with bunk beds for napping, younger children sat on a pink-and-blue mat, captivated by a teacher reading them a story.
“We spend more time in shelter than in classrooms,” Kurinna sighed.
As comfortable as their shelters were, after two hours underground, the all-clear signal was met with a wave of enthusiasm.
Anya, Yasya and Varvara finished their English class before dashing out to enjoy a 15-minute break in the fresh autumn sun.
“Freedom!” Anya said in English, before the girls joined classmates playing with a huge red, yellow and blue balloon. — AFP
